# Investigation Report: HyperFund / HyperVerse Alleged Crypto Fraud Network

## Executive assessment

The available evidence supports a coherent assessment that HyperFund—and its subsequent iterations HyperVerse and HyperNation—used a combination of unusually high promised returns, multilevel recruitment incentives, internal crypto-accounting mechanisms, public-facing promoters, repeated rebranding, and credibility-focused marketing to attract and retain investors. The SEC characterizes the operation as both a pyramid and Ponzi scheme, alleging that investor withdrawals were funded primarily by newer deposits rather than legitimate mining or other operating revenue. The DOJ similarly alleges that the scheme promised returns supposedly generated by large-scale cryptocurrency mining that did not exist. These remain allegations in the SEC civil complaint and in the criminal cases unless established by final judgment, although the DOJ reports that Brenda Chunga pleaded guilty and that Rodney Burton was later sentenced. [S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases) [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)

The network’s apparent operating model was not simply an investment website. It was an integrated promotional system. The core proposition was passive income: investors purchased “memberships” using Tether and were promised daily rewards of approximately 0.5% to 1%, potentially reaching two or three times—or, in some versions, four times—the initial investment. At the same time, participants were encouraged to recruit others through commissions, downline structures, VIP classifications, and pooled “global” rewards. This combination created both an investment narrative and a social-distribution mechanism. [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11) [S3](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html)

In my assessment, the most significant feature of the alleged scheme was the interaction between these elements. High returns supplied the initial attraction; recruitment rewards expanded distribution; public promoters supplied trust and urgency; rebranding helped preserve the appearance of continuity when withdrawal problems emerged; and the questionable “Steven Reece Lewis” persona supplied a fresh executive image for HyperVerse. The evidence therefore points to an alleged credibility-and-recruitment architecture rather than an isolated false statement or failed crypto venture.

## Sources and evidentiary hierarchy

The primary sources are the SEC complaint and DOJ case page. The SEC complaint provides detailed allegations, quoted promotional statements, transaction mechanics, dates, and claimed amounts. The DOJ page provides the criminal case status and identifies the relevant defendants and charges. CNBC is a secondary report summarizing the January 29, 2024 DOJ and SEC announcements. The Guardian provides investigative reporting on the apparent nonexistence of the HyperVerse CEO persona and contextual information about promotional videos and celebrity messages.

| Source ID | Source type | Main evidentiary contribution |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | U.S. Department of Justice case page | Criminal defendants, charges, plea and sentencing updates, alleged scheme timeline |
| S2 | SEC civil complaint | Detailed mechanics, alleged misrepresentations, promoter conduct, CEO persona, amounts |
| S3 | CNBC report | Contemporaneous summary of DOJ and SEC enforcement announcements |
| S4 | The Guardian investigation | Independent reporting on “Steven Reece Lewis,” launch videos, celebrity endorsements, and investor experience |

The SEC and DOJ sources should receive the greatest weight for allegations and procedural status because they are official court and government materials. The Guardian is valuable for independent corroboration of the questionable CEO persona and promotional environment, but some of its findings are necessarily investigative and should not be treated as judicial determinations. [S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases) [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11) [S4](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist)

## The alleged investment and Ponzi mechanics

### Memberships and promised returns

According to the SEC complaint, HyperFund launched in June 2020 and sold “membership” packages denominated internally as HyperUnits. Investors generally used Tether, or in some cases paid U.S. dollars to promoters. The complaint identifies example membership levels of $300, $500, $1,000, and $10,000. [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)

The central promise was a passive daily reward of 0.5% to 1% of the investment, allegedly continuing until the investor had earned as much as three times the original amount over 600 days. The SEC complaint quotes Chunga telling prospective investors that they could recover their original investment in approximately seven months and then treat subsequent payments as “pure profit.” [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)

The DOJ describes the same basic promise, stating that investors were told their returns would be paid from large-scale cryptocurrency mining operations. The DOJ alleges that those mining operations did not exist. [S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases) The SEC complaint likewise alleges that HyperFund had no legitimate revenue source sufficient to support the promised returns and that investor withdrawals were funded by newer investor deposits. [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)

This alleged structure contains the defining economic risk of a Ponzi arrangement: promised returns are detached from verifiable operating revenue and depend on continued inflows. The claim should be stated cautiously, because the “Ponzi” characterization is an allegation by the SEC and DOJ rather than an independent accounting finding presented in the supplied materials.

### Recruitment incentives and pyramid characteristics

The alleged scheme also had a pyramid-style distribution structure. Investors could obtain “accelerated” or leveraged rewards by recruiting new participants. The SEC complaint describes Community Rewards allegedly paid through as many as 20 levels of a recruiter's downline. It also describes VIP Rewards tied to team sales and Global Rewards based on a pool said to equal 4% of company sales. [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)

This design gave promoters a reason to emphasize recruitment rather than independently verifiable business performance. Chunga allegedly reached “VIP 5 STAR,” the highest promotional level, after generating at least $5 million in new investment sales. The SEC alleges that she received approximately $2.5 million in withdrawals from the platform and approximately $1.1 million directly from investors, for total receipts of approximately $3.7 million. [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)

The recruitment structure also appears to have converted personal reputation into a sales tool. The SEC alleges that Chunga displayed wealth, made promotional videos, hosted Zoom presentations, and used expensive possessions and lifestyle claims to encourage others to join. The complaint alleges that she claimed to be earning more than $5 million annually from a crypto platform, although the SEC says that statement was false. [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)

## Internal crypto mechanics and withdrawal constraints

The alleged scheme used internal units and crypto conversions that could make the investment appear liquid while complicating actual redemption. A membership’s nominal value was represented as HyperUnits, but withdrawals allegedly required converting those units into Molecular Future tokens, or MOF, and then moving the MOF through the HOO Exchange before conversion into other crypto assets or fiat currency. [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)

The SEC complaint alleges that HyperUnits were shown as pegged to one dollar when deposited but were not protected at that value when converted to MOF for withdrawal. It further states that MOF had fallen to approximately $0.00001949 by September 4, 2023, although the complaint acknowledges that it did not appear to be actively traded at that point. [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)

This mechanism matters because it could preserve the appearance of account growth while making redemption economically impractical. The reported value inside the platform did not necessarily correspond to cash that investors could obtain outside it. In analytical terms, the alleged structure separated nominal account value from realizable value.

Withdrawal problems reportedly intensified during the transition from HyperFund to HyperVerse. The SEC alleges that investors experienced difficulty withdrawing in November and December 2021 and were unable to withdraw by February or March 2022. The HOO Exchange reportedly suspended withdrawals in June 2022 and stopped functioning by November 2022. [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11) The DOJ page states that withdrawals began to be blocked at least by July 2021, while CNBC reports the same allegation. [S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases) [S3](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html)

## Public promoters and credibility engineering

### Promoter-led distribution

The evidence indicates that promoters were central to distribution. The SEC alleges that Chunga was one of the most prominent U.S. promoters and one of only two U.S.-based “corporate” presenters. She allegedly used recurring Zoom presentations, PowerPoint materials, social media, referral links, and direct payment arrangements to recruit investors. [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)

The promotional message combined passive rewards with assurances about organizational legitimacy. The SEC complaint states that materials highlighted Lee’s media appearances, Blockchain Global, purported corporate affiliations, and other “credibility” indicators. Chunga allegedly told prospective investors that the founders had “more to lose than to gain” and that the company did not need investors’ money. [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)

This is important because the alleged fraud did not rely solely on technical crypto claims. It also relied on social proof: visible promoters, a hierarchy of ranks, public presentations, founder biographies, and apparent institutional connections.

### Alleged false affiliations and mining claims

The SEC alleges that promotional materials falsely presented DigitalX as part of the HyperTech Group. DigitalX reportedly issued a notice in February 2021 disavowing any association with HyperTech Group, HyperFund, and related projects. The complaint also alleges that promotional materials claimed an IBM relationship involving Hcash, although IBM was not involved with Hcash. [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)

The mining narrative was particularly important because it purported to explain how the daily rewards could be paid. Chunga allegedly described warehouses operating around the world and generating millions through continuous crypto mining. The SEC complaint alleges that Lee later acknowledged that the group had exited bitcoin mining in 2019 and did not own mining machines thereafter. It further alleges that Lee knew the promotional mining narrative was inaccurate but did not correct it. [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)

If proven, these facts would show that the mining story was not incidental advertising but the alleged economic justification for the promised passive rewards.

## Rebranding as a continuity and recruitment tactic

HyperFund was reportedly rebranded as HyperVerse in late 2021 and then as HyperNation in approximately May 2022. The SEC complaint describes the projects as successive versions of the same broader operation. [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)

The HyperVerse rebrand shifted the marketing language toward a virtual world or metaverse. The new version allegedly promised similar rewards, while also adding a “university-level blockchain education” and a new native token narrative. HyperVerse 2.0 reportedly changed the returns to 0.3% daily and increased the maximum advertised multiple to four times the initial investment over 1,333 days. [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)

HyperNation introduced a more ideological presentation involving decentralization, inequality, and a masked figure called “Mr. H.” Membership packages were reportedly represented as NFT boxes, and the SEC alleges that a $10,000 NFT was required to transfer a participant’s downline from HyperVerse to HyperNation. [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)

The sequence suggests an alleged continuity strategy: when the prior version faced withdrawal problems, the branding and narrative changed while the underlying member relationships and recruitment logic continued. The Guardian reported that a senior promoter described HyperVerse and HyperNation as “one big entity,” although the supplied material does not establish that this statement was made by an owner or legal entity. [S4](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist)

## The questionable “Steven Reece Lewis” CEO persona

The HyperVerse launch introduced a purported CEO named Steven Reece Lewis. The SEC alleges that this person was not a real CEO but a paid actor presenting a fabricated character. It further alleges that the actor worked as a television presenter and lived in Bangkok. [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)

The Guardian independently reported that the claimed educational and employment history could not be verified. It stated that the Universities of Leeds and Cambridge had no record of the individual under that name, that no relevant Companies House or SEC records were found, and that Goldman Sachs could not identify a record of his employment. The Guardian also reported that Adobe had no public record of acquiring a company owned by him. [S4](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist)

The CEO persona therefore appears to have served a specific promotional purpose: it gave the rebranded project a new executive identity and a biography designed to imply conventional business competence. The SEC alleges that Lee knew or recklessly disregarded that the presented individual was not the genuine CEO. [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)

The launch was supplemented by celebrity messages from Steve Wozniak, Chuck Norris, Jim Norton, and Lance Bass. The Guardian reported that the messages encouraged support for HyperVerse but did not refer directly to investments, and that the celebrities were available through Cameo. The Guardian also stated there was no suggestion that they knew the scheme’s business model. [S4](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist)

## Scale, legal status, and contradictions

The sources use different estimates for the amount raised:

| Source | Amount | Characterization |
|---|---:|---|
| SEC complaint | More than $1.7 billion | Alleged amount raised worldwide |
| DOJ case page | Approximately $1.89 billion | Alleged criminal scheme amount |
| CNBC | Approximately $1.9 billion | Reported DOJ figure |
| Guardian citing Chainalysis | $1.3 billion in consumer losses during 2022 | Estimate of losses, not necessarily total funds raised |

These figures are not necessarily irreconcilable because they may measure different things: total funds raised, alleged criminal proceeds, or estimated consumer losses. They should not be merged into a single precise figure. [S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases) [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11) [S3](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html) [S4](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist)

The procedural posture also requires care. The DOJ page reports that Sam Lee was indicted, Brenda Chunga pleaded guilty, and Rodney Burton was charged. It additionally reports that Burton was sentenced on July 23, 2026, to 32 months’ imprisonment and three years of supervised release. The same page continues to describe Lee’s indictment and Chunga’s case within the criminal proceeding. [S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases)

## Conclusion

The strongest evidence-based conclusion is that HyperFund/HyperVerse allegedly combined a high-yield investment promise with a multilevel recruitment engine and a credibility-management campaign. The claimed mining revenue supplied an apparent economic explanation for the returns; internal HyperUnits and token conversions created the appearance of account value; promoters translated the model into personal recommendations and lifestyle demonstrations; rebranding helped maintain organizational momentum; and the questionable CEO persona added a manufactured executive identity during the HyperVerse phase.

The allegations are especially significant because these components reinforced one another. A new investor was not merely shown a website promising crypto rewards. The investor could encounter a promoter, a rank-based compensation plan, founder biographies, purported corporate affiliations, a mining narrative, a new metaverse brand, celebrity videos, and a supposedly accomplished CEO. In my assessment, the evidence is consistent with an alleged system designed to manufacture trust and sustain inflows while obscuring the absence of legitimate revenue. The ultimate legal conclusions remain governed by the criminal and civil proceedings, but the supplied record provides substantial support for describing the network as an alleged crypto Ponzi/pyramid operation employing rebranding and staged credibility.

## References
